facts.text: On this date in 1920, the Treaty of Sèvres partitioned the Ottoman Empire — a map that never held. Turkey rejected it, fought back, and redrew its own borders by 1923.
On August 10, 1948, Candid Camera premiered on US television, making ordinary Americans the subject of mass media for the first time.
Mongolia has more horses than people. With 3.5 million residents and roughly 4.3 million horses, it is the only country on Earth where the livestock-to-human ratio tips that way for a single species.
Vatican City generates more income per square meter than any nation on Earth, driven almost entirely by museum admissions, postage stamps, and donations — not taxes.

The Democratic Republic of Congo sits above an estimated $24 trillion in untapped mineral wealth, more than the combined GDP of the US and EU, yet ranks among the world's poorest countries by per capita income.
On this day in 1792, the storming of the Tuileries palace triggered France's first sovereign debt default — investors holding royal bonds lost everything within weeks.
On August 10, 1949, Congress officially made the Department of Defense permanent, locking in what Eisenhower would later call the military-industrial complex's financial engine.
The S&P 500 has historically returned more in the four months following a presidential election than in the eight months preceding one, regardless of which party wins.
Berkshire Hathaway's share price has never split its Class A stock — one share now costs over $700,000, making it the highest-priced stock on any major exchange.
Japan's government pension fund, GPIF, manages $1.5 trillion — more than the GDP of Australia — making it the single largest pool of retirement money on Earth.
On this date in 1990, the Magellan spacecraft entered Venus's orbit — where it discovered a surface so volcanically resurfaced that no terrain there is older than 500 million years.
On August 10, 1675, the Royal Observatory at Greenwich was founded — the building was positioned not for science, but to fit the footprint of a demolished castle.
Your skeleton is not static. Bone tissue is constantly dissolved and rebuilt, replacing itself entirely roughly every decade throughout your adult life.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. A teaspoon of its material would weigh about a billion tons on Earth.
Mantis shrimp see with 16 types of photoreceptors — yet research shows they process color worse than humans, using the channels as binary triggers rather than mixing them.
On this day in 1628, the Swedish warship Vasa sank 1,300 meters into her maiden voyage. She was underwater longer than the United States has existed.
Missouri became the 24th U.S. state on August 10, 1821. Beethoven was still alive, composing his final symphonies.
The fax machine was patented in 1843 — 33 years before the telephone. Alexander Graham Bell was not yet born when faxing was theoretically possible.
Oxford University is older than the Aztec Empire. Lectures began at Oxford around 1096; Tenochtitlan wasn't founded until 1325.
On this day in 1846, the Smithsonian Institution was established. The institution is now older than the light currently reaching us from many stars visible tonight.
Sonder (n.): the realization that each passerby has a life as vivid and complex as your own. Coined by John Koenig in The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, 2012 — and already feels ancient.
Hiraeth (n.): a Welsh word for a longing for home that may never have existed. It folds homesickness, grief, and nostalgia into a single breath English cannot match.
On this day in 1628, the Swedish warship Vasa sank minutes into her maiden voyage. The Swedish word 'vasa' means sheaf of grain — an irony the sea apparently found fitting.
Petrichor (n.): the smell of rain on dry earth. Coined in 1964 by Australian scientists Isabel Bear and R.G. Thomas, from Greek petra (stone) and ichor (the fluid in the veins of the gods).

On this day in 1519, Magellan's fleet departed Seville to circumnavigate the globe. The Portuguese verb 'malhar' — to strike, to push through — shares a root with the relentless momentum that defined him.

On this date in 2010, Bitcoin Pizza Day's afterglow was fading — but August 10, 2012 brought the Bitcoin Savings & Trust Ponzi indictment, the first major U.S. federal securities fraud case built entirely on blockchain transaction records.
On August 10, 2021, Poly Network was drained of $611M across three chains simultaneously. The attacker then returned every dollar, claiming they did it 'for fun' and to expose the vulnerability.
Ethereum's gas limit is not set by code — it's a rolling miner (now validator) vote, adjusted each block by up to 1/1024th. The 'limit' is effectively a continuous, decentralized negotiation.
Satoshi's original Bitcoin codebase contained a hidden alert system that let a single private key broadcast network-wide messages to all nodes — a secret superuser backdoor quietly removed in 2016.
The Bitcoin UTXO set — every unspent coin's location — fits entirely in RAM on a laptop. As of 2026 it remains under 12GB, meaning global monetary state is smaller than a Netflix download queue.

On this date in 2006, Geoffrey Hinton and Ruslan Salakhutdinov published 'Reducing the Dimensionality of Data with Neural Networks' in Science — quietly relaunching deep learning after a decade of dormancy.

On this date in 2012, the Google Brain cat-neuron paper appeared on arXiv: an unsupervised network trained on YouTube frames spontaneously developed a face detector using 16,000 CPU cores and zero labels.
GPT-4's training run is estimated to have consumed roughly 50 GWh of electricity — comparable to the annual consumption of 4,500 average US homes, for a single model training pass.

AlphaFold 2 predicted structures for over 200 million proteins before most wet labs had processed a few hundred. The entire UniProt database now has coverage, a task that would have taken classical methods geological timescales.

The transformer architecture, now underlying virtually every frontier AI system, was introduced in 2017 by a team of eight — six of whom had left Google within five years to found or co-found competing AI labs.
